title: Philippine Arts & Cultural Symbols
subtitle: Design with a job. And what each symbol carries.
objectives: Name the main Philippine cultural symbols
Say which group or region each comes from
Explain the meaning each symbol carries
Read the symbols on the national flag

cards.title: A symbol stops being a symbol when you call it a pattern
cards.text: Every one of these means something specific to the people who made it. Learn the meaning and the design stops being wallpaper.

cards.title: Design with a job
cards.text: None of these were made to look nice on a shirt.
points: **Sarimanok** marks rank and fortune.
**Bulul** guards a rice harvest.
**T'nalak** records a dream.
**Okir** says whose house this is.

cards.title: Six symbols, and what each one carries
cards.text: Tap each symbol. The second line is what it carries.

question.text: The t'nalak is woven by the…
question.explain: From abaca, in red, black and white, in South Cotabato.

cards.title: Dreamed, then woven
cards.text: The process is the reason the cloth matters.
points: **The fibre is abaca**, stripped and knotted by hand.
**Three colours only:** red, black, white.
**The weaver is called a dreamweaver**: the pattern comes in a dream.
**Months per piece.** It is not printed.

cards.title: The flag, part by part
cards.text: Tap each part. The last button is the one most people do not know.

question.text: What do the three stars on the flag stand for?

cards.title: The jeepney is a moving artwork
cards.text: Nowhere else is a public vehicle also the owner's portrait.
points: **Chrome horses** on the bonnet.
**His children's names** along the side.
**A saint, a team, a hometown**: all of it chosen.
**Same instinct as okir:** mark what is yours.

cards.title: Borrowed symbols get their meaning stripped
cards.text: Games take designs from real cultures, and often lose what they meant.
points: **A pattern used as decoration** carries nothing.
**The same pattern on a torogan** says rank and ownership.
**Ask where a design came from.**
**That question is the whole point** of this week.

cards.title: A parol is a star somebody built
cards.text: San Fernando's giant lanterns run on their own motors and crews.
points: **Metres across**, with thousands of bulbs.
**Switched in sequence** so the light appears to move.
**Barangays compete** every December.
**It began as a simple star lantern.** It became engineering.

cards.title: Four things that mean something
cards.alt: Handwoven red, black and cream abaca cloth, a star-shaped capiz lantern, a carved leaf-and-vine wood panel and a small carved wooden figure
cards.text: Woven cloth, a star lantern, carved scrollwork, a standing figure. Say what each one carries.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Sarimanok and okir: Maranao. Bulul: Ifugao. T'nalak: T'boli.
T'nalak is abaca, three colours, and the pattern is dreamed.
Flag: 8 rays for 8 provinces, 3 stars for the island groups.
Ask of any design: where is it from, and what does it mean?

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 5 MAPEH, Arts strand. The organising claim is that each of these designs was made to do something (mark rank, guard a harvest, record a dream, say whose house this is) and that calling it a pattern is what empties it. T'nalak gets a card of its own because the process, including the dreamweaver, is the reason the cloth matters and is the detail most likely to stick. The flag explorer from Term 1 returns here, which is deliberate: it is the one set of symbols he will be asked about for the rest of his schooling, and the war-inversion fact is genuinely little known. The gaming lens turns the week into a transferable habit: ask where a design came from.
discussion: Ask which group each symbol belongs to.
Ask why the weaver is called a dreamweaver.
Ask what the eight rays stand for.
Ask what a jeepney's paintwork tells you about its owner.
extension: Have him design a symbol for himself and say what every part means.
Have him look at a jeepney and list everything the owner chose.
misconceptions: "These are just patterns." Each one carries a specific meaning.
"The three stars are three heroes." Luzon, Visayas, Mindanao.
"T'nalak is printed cloth." Hand-woven abaca, months per piece.
